title: Webhook Authentication and Reliability
learning_outcomes: Explain how webhook authentication and reliability affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from signature verification to a concrete API example.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on webhook authentication and reliability in asynchronous apis, webhooks, and external integrations. You will connect signature verification to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: Webhook Authentication and Reliability matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying signature verification deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: External work needs bounded timeouts, verified webhooks, duplicate-event handling, observable job status, and recovery logic. In this lesson, treat “Webhook Authentication and Reliability” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

content_blocks.text: Start with “Signature verification”; it establishes the vocabulary for this topic. Next, compare it with “Replay protection” and “Retry schedules and dead-letter handling”. troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating webhook authentication and reliability as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
